newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee surges, powered by heavy funds demand.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee surges, powered by heavy funds demand.

text.p: LIFFE robusta coffee futures, driven by day-long trade, funds and speculative short-covering, motored sharply higher in heavy volume on Wednesday.
"The buying was constant throughout the day," said one.

Volume was an impressive 16,733 lots, the highest level in many months, with buyers rushing in as London chased the sharp New York advance on Tuesday after what some termed as bullish crop news from Brazil.
Most-active March, rebounding from Tuesday's life-low of $1,203 a tonne, finished $76 firmer on the day at $1,303.
It had scaled a session high of $1,312, the highest level last seen on November 29 last year.
Traders said the contract now looked set to bottom out around this level and make a move towards $1,355-$1,400 in the immediate term.
Funds buy-stops were seen after March whizzed past the $1,280 mark, a break above a major downtrend line in place since September last year. About 1,000 lots were done at that level.
"The main shorts are funds and I think they had to buy back something because it's becoming rather costly," said one trader.
Traders said Ivory Coast and Vietnam selling was seen in the morning but it dried out later in the day.
One trader said: "I think people that bought today were not volunteer buyers but were obliged to buy back something. When this buying disappears, I don't think roasters will buy immediately."
The heavy gains prompted the clearing house to ask short holders to pay up an intra-day margin of US$400 a lot with immediate effect.
New York surged to seven-month-high on Tuesdsay on the back of bullish Brazilian crop news and an unexpected drawdwon in U.S. certified stocks.

But some traders in London were puzzled by positive New York reaction to the news that Brazil's 1997/98 crop could hover around 19 million 60-kg bags. "This unofficial estimate followed earlier Brazil growers' forecast of an even lower crop of 17 million and yet the market goes this sort of way," one said.
